note: RUBRIC_SLIM_SPEC batch: old U2 L4-8 (scatterplots, r, regression, residuals, LSRL; NEW Unit 5). CB regression FRQs score: slope interpreted in context with 'predicted' and 'for each one unit'; r / r-squared interpreted in context; residual = actual - predicted with its sign read as over/under-prediction; extrapolation named with the reason. Applied with scripts/rubric-slim-apply.mjs. Revised after the Codex review: requested statistical ideas restored under the cap-5 rule; P and I made disjoint (I = neither idea / central idea wrong).

scoringGuide.E: Explains that the explanatory variable is the one used to predict or explain the response, and that it goes on the x-axis (so the response goes on y).
scoringGuide.P: Gives the explain/predict role but places the variables on the wrong axes, or gives correct axis placement with no explain/predict idea.
scoringGuide.I: Neither the roles nor the axis placement is correct.

scoringGuide.E: Explains that 'positive' is only the direction, and a complete description also gives form (linear or not), strength, and unusual features, in the context of the variables.
scoringGuide.P: Two of form, strength, and features/context are named; one is missing.
scoringGuide.I: Only direction is discussed, or the parts of a description are not named.

scoringGuide.E: Hours studied is explanatory and quiz score is the response (with the reason); a scatterplot fits because each student supplies a pair of quantitative values; and the likely relationship is described as positive, roughly linear, and fairly strong, in context. The construction features strengthen the answer.
scoringGuide.P: Four of the five are correct; one is missing or wrong.
scoringGuide.I: Two or more of the five are missing or wrong, or the variables' roles are swapped.

scoringGuide.E: The sign of r gives the direction (positive: y tends to rise with x; negative: falls) and the distance from 0 gives the strength of the linear relationship (near 1 or -1 strong, near 0 weak). Either half can be stated in either wording.
scoringGuide.P: Explains sign or magnitude correctly but not both.
scoringGuide.I: Neither sign nor magnitude is interpreted correctly.

scoringGuide.E: States that correlation does not imply causation, and that r alone does not show the form of the relationship (or unusual features), so the scatterplot is still needed.
scoringGuide.P: Gives the no-causation idea but not what r fails to show, or says what r cannot show while treating the relationship as causal.
scoringGuide.I: Neither idea is present: r is treated as both proof of causation and a complete description.

scoringGuide.E: Interprets r = 0.89 as a strong positive linear relationship in context (more tutoring tends to go with higher quiz scores), names one thing r alone does not show (form or unusual features), and explains why it does not prove tutoring causes higher scores. The technology reason strengthens the answer.
scoringGuide.P: Three of the four are correct; one is missing or wrong.
scoringGuide.I: Two or more of the four are missing or wrong.

scoringGuide.E: Explains that the x-value is multiplied by the slope and added to the intercept to get y-hat, and that y-hat is a predicted value, not the exact observed response.
scoringGuide.P: Describes the arithmetic without saying the result is only a prediction, or says it is a prediction without describing how the equation produces it.
scoringGuide.I: Neither idea is present, or y-hat is treated as the actual observed value with no arithmetic.

scoringGuide.E: Defines extrapolation as predicting for an x outside the range of observed x-values, and explains it is risky because the pattern may not continue there. Deciding = comparing the x to the observed interval, which the definition carries.
scoringGuide.P: Names extrapolation (predicting outside the observed x-range) without the reason it is risky, or gives the risk without saying what extrapolation is.

scoringGuide.E: Slope: predicted quiz score rises 1.8 points per additional hour of tutoring; intercept: predicted score 61.4 with 0 hours; y-hat = 61.4 + 1.8(8) = 75.8 with the substitution shown; the prediction is not exact because individual students vary around the line; x = 15 is outside 2-10 hours, so it is extrapolation and not reliable.
scoringGuide.P: Four of the five are correct; one is missing or wrong (commonly a slope with no 'predicted' or no 'per hour').
scoringGuide.I: Two or more of the five are missing or wrong.

scoringGuide.E: Residual = actual - predicted for one point, and a positive residual means the actual value was above the prediction (model underestimated); negative is the reverse. Stating the positive case with its meaning is enough; the negative case follows.
scoringGuide.P: Defines the residual without reading its sign, or reads the sign without defining the residual.
scoringGuide.I: Neither idea is present, or the residual is defined backwards with the sign read wrongly.

scoringGuide.E: A residual plot with random scatter and no pattern supports a linear model; a visible pattern such as curvature means the linear model may not be appropriate. Mentioning scatter around zero strengthens the answer.
scoringGuide.P: Gives the good sign without the warning sign, or the warning sign without the good sign.
scoringGuide.I: Neither is present, or the residual plot is not connected to model fit.

scoringGuide.E: Residual 84 - 51.4 = 32.6, meaning the store had 32.6 more organic items than the model predicted, so the model underpredicted; random scatter around zero with no pattern means a linear model is appropriate; a curved or systematic pattern would make a linear model questionable.
scoringGuide.P: Four of the five are correct; one is missing or wrong.
scoringGuide.I: Two or more of the five are missing or wrong, or the residual is computed backwards.

scoringGuide.E: Explains that residuals are squared so positive and negative errors cannot cancel, and that the LSRL is the line minimizing the sum of squared residuals. The (x-bar, y-bar) and slope-formula properties strengthen the answer.
scoringGuide.P: Gives one of the two ideas (why residuals are squared, or what the LSRL minimizes).

scoringGuide.E: Interprets a slope in context as the predicted change in the response for each one-unit increase in the explanatory variable (any suitable context; the attendance example is one), interprets the intercept as the predicted response when the explanatory variable is 0, and explains that the intercept is not meaningful when x = 0 is outside a sensible range or gives an impossible prediction. Bare definitions with no variables named do not earn E.
scoringGuide.P: Two of the three are correct; one is missing, muddled, or given without context.
scoringGuide.I: Fewer than two are correct (e.g. slope and intercept both misinterpreted).

scoringGuide.E: r-squared = the proportion of variation in the response explained by the linear relationship with the explanatory variable; in computer output the slope is the coefficient on the explanatory variable and the intercept is the constant. The 90.3% example strengthens the answer.
scoringGuide.P: Two of the three are correct; one is missing or muddled.
scoringGuide.I: Fewer than two are correct (e.g. r-squared misread AND the output not read).

scoringGuide.E: Residuals are squared so errors do not cancel and the LSRL minimizes their sum; slope 0.57: predicted questions correct rise 0.57 per 1-percentage-point increase in attendance; the intercept -7.69 is the predicted score at 0% attendance and is not meaningful because 0% is unreasonable and the prediction is impossible; 0.903 means 90.3% of the variation in questions correct is explained by the linear relationship with attendance; (x-bar, y-bar) lies on the line.
scoringGuide.P: Four of the five are correct; one is missing or wrong.
scoringGuide.I: Two or more of the five are missing or wrong.
